final_writeup:
The target is proved unconditionally for every c≤e. For arbitrary c, the greedy construction gives an exact polynomial-time triage and additional YES/NO cases.

There is also a strong complexity barrier. A radius-n/c sidestep solver yields a polynomial-time dominating set within additive 2n/c of optimum. On maximum-degree-six graphs this is a (1+14/c)-approximation. An explicit degree-six gadget transfers such approximations to cubic Vertex Cover without loss. Hence the universal target would produce a PTAS family for cubic Vertex Cover. Under its standard APX-hardness theorem, the universal target is equivalent to P=NP: P=NP trivially permits H=G, while for P≠NP every sufficiently large fixed c is impossible.

Thus no unconditional resolution for all c is claimed. The remaining unconditional regime is c>e, particularly instances whose greedy residual lies between n/c and n(1-1/q)^q and which lack the sparse NO certificates below.

results.claim: For 0≤q≤n, a graph has a dominating set of exactly q vertices if and only if its domination number γ is at most q.
results.proof_sketch: One direction is immediate. Conversely, any dominating set of size at most q can be extended with arbitrary unused vertices; supersets of dominating sets remain dominating.

results.claim: Greedy closed-neighborhood coverage has residual r≤n(1-1/q)^q whenever γ(G)≤q, for q≥1.
results.proof_sketch: Let U be the currently uncovered vertices and let D be a q-vertex dominating set. The sets N[d]∩U for d∈D cover U, so one has size at least |U|/q. A previously selected vertex has zero intersection with U, hence greedy can select an unselected vertex with this gain. Thus |U_i|≤(1-1/q)|U_{i-1}|. Iterating q times gives r q^q≤n(q-1)^q. Therefore an observed violation certifies γ(G)>q.

results.claim: For arbitrary fixed c, greedy gives an exact polynomial-time triage: it solves the instance whenever r≤n/c or r>n(1-1/q)^q.
results.proof_sketch: If r≤n/c, fix a greedy-selected vertex s and add su for every residual vertex u. Such edges are absent from G, are distinct, and make the selected q-set dominate. If r exceeds the theoretical bound, the preceding lemma proves that G itself has no q-dominating set, so output (G,nil). Integer powers permit the theoretical comparison in polynomial-time exact arithmetic.

results.claim: Sidestep(Dominating Set,dist_e,n/c) is in FP for every fixed c≤e.
results.proof_sketch: For q=0, output the empty set when n=0 and nil otherwise. For q≥1 run the preceding triage. Since ln(1-1/q)≤-1/q, the theoretical residual bound is at most n/e≤n/c. Hence either the residual violates the bound, certifying nil for G, or all residual vertices can be repaired within the permitted radius.

results.claim: For every c, all instances with q≥1 and n-q≤n/c have a direct polynomial-time YES output.
results.proof_sketch: Choose any q-set S. At most n-q vertices lie outside S; add one edge from a fixed s∈S to each vertex not already dominated by S. This uses at most n-q edits and makes S dominating.

results.claim: For every c, a computable sparse NO certificate is available when q+1 vertices have at most n/c incident edges in total.
results.proof_sketch: Delete every edge incident with those q+1 vertices. They become isolated, so every dominating set of the resulting graph contains all q+1 and no q-set exists. In particular, this applies whenever the sum of the q+1 smallest vertex degrees is at most n/c.

results.claim: Domination number is one-Lipschitz per edge edit, with a constructive transfer.
results.proof_sketch: Let S dominate H and let U be the vertices not dominated by S in G. For each u∈U, domination in H supplies an edge su in E(H) minus E(G). Distinct u require distinct edges, so |U|≤|E(H) minus E(G)|, and S∪U dominates G. Reversing G,H gives |γ(G)-γ(H)|≤|E(G) symmetric-difference E(H)|.

results.claim: A radius-R sidestep solver decides every additive-gap instance whose YES case has γ(G)≤q-R and whose NO case has γ(G)>q+R.
results.proof_sketch: The Lipschitz lemma implies that every graph H within radius R has γ(H)≤q in the YES case and γ(H)>q in the NO case. Thus the solver's output type is invariant throughout the radius-R ball. In particular, a constant-fraction promise gap a<b is decided by choosing q near (a+b)n/2 whenever 2/c<b-a; rounding is absorbed for sufficiently large n.

results.claim: Any FP solver at fixed c yields a polynomial-time additive-2⌊n/c⌋ approximation for Minimum Dominating Set.
results.proof_sketch: Put R=⌊n/c⌋ and call the solver for every q=0,…,n. Let q* be the least threshold producing a set S in some H. A YES must occur by q≤min(n,γ(G)+R), since γ(H)≤γ(G)+R. Transfer S to G using at most R extra vertices. The resulting dominating set has size at most q*+R≤γ(G)+2R.

results.claim: On graphs of maximum degree Δ, the preceding algorithm is a (1+2(Δ+1)/c)-approximation.
results.proof_sketch: Every dominator covers at most Δ+1 vertices, hence γ(G)≥n/(Δ+1). Therefore γ(G)+2n/c≤(1+2(Δ+1)/c)γ(G).

results.claim: There is an exact approximation-preserving reduction from isolate-free Vertex Cover of maximum degree three to Dominating Set of maximum degree six.
results.proof_sketch: For F, retain every original edge uv and add a vertex x_e adjacent to u and v for each edge e=uv. A vertex cover C dominates the gadget: it dominates every x_e, and each original vertex outside C has a neighbor in C. Conversely, replace each selected x_e in any dominating set by one endpoint. This preserves domination and never increases size; the resulting original-vertex set must cover every edge because it dominates x_e. Thus γ(gadget)=τ(F), and original degrees double to at most six.

results.claim: The universal target implies a PTAS family for cubic Minimum Vertex Cover.
results.proof_sketch: Given accuracy ε>0, use the asserted solver with fixed c=14/ε. Apply the additive algorithm to the degree-six gadget. The maximum-degree bound gives a (1+ε)-approximate dominating set, which the gadget conversion maps to a no-larger vertex cover while preserving the optimum.

results.claim: Conditional on the standard APX-hardness theorem for cubic Vertex Cover, the universal target holds if and only if P=NP.
results.proof_sketch: APX-hardness supplies η>0 such that a (1+η)-approximation for cubic Vertex Cover would imply P=NP. Thus any sidestep solver with c>14/η would imply P=NP, so under P≠NP the claimed algorithms cannot exist for all c. Conversely, if P=NP, decide and construct a q-dominating set of G in polynomial time, extend it to exactly q when it exists, and always output H=G; this works for every c with zero edits.
